title_en: Fragments on the Letter to the Philippians
author: Severianus of Gabala
occasion: Severianus comments on selected verses of Paul's Letter to the Philippians, explaining difficult expressions and defending the coherence of Paul's argument.
argument: Severianus opens by arguing that Paul wrote Philippians to clergy, not laity, and that his main aim was to instill humility in them, since pride especially afflicts those who live well. He then explains Paul's appeals to the Philippians' faith and steadfastness as proof that his sufferings and defense of the gospel are not fruitless. In commenting on Philippians 2:7, he insists that 'as' (ὡς) expresses intensity, not mere likeness. He interprets Paul's counting his former gains as loss and rubbish through an extended agricultural image: Abraham's faith is like the seed producing the root of the law, the stalk of the prophets, and the grain that is Christ, while the chaff-like elements of the law were separated at Christ's first coming. Finally, he clarifies that Paul's forgetting what lies behind does not mean his past labors were evil, and he notes a tradition identifying Euodia as the jailer's wife and Syntyche as the man, likely the jailer himself.

outline.move: Severianus states that Paul wrote to clergy, not laity, and that his purpose was to instill humility, since pride especially attacks those who live well.

He explains that Paul uses the Philippians' faith and steadfastness as proof that his sufferings and defense of the gospel are not fruitless, and he interprets 'as' in Philippians 2:7 as expressing intensity rather than mere likeness.

He develops an agricultural image in which Abraham's faith is like the seed producing the root of the law, the stalk of the prophets, and the grain that is Christ; the harvest and threshing occur at Christ's first coming.

He concludes the agricultural image by clarifying that the stalk of the law did not cease, but circumcision, sabbath-keeping and other things were separated like chaff, and the pure grain of faith hidden in the prophetic stalk was stored in the master's barns; he also explains Paul's forgetting what lies behind and notes a tradition about Euodia and Syntyche.

cast.name: Paul
cast.who: The apostle and author of the letter being commented on.

cast.name: Timothy
cast.who: Paul's co-worker, mentioned as the recipient of similar advice.

cast.name: Abraham
cast.who: The patriarch whose faith is the seed from which the law, prophets, and Christ grew.

cast.name: Euodia
cast.who: One of the two people Paul urges to agree in Philippians 4:2; some say she was the jailer's wife.

cast.name: Syntyche
cast.who: The other person Paul urges to agree; some say he was the man, likely the jailer himself.

voices.speaker: Paul (quoted)
voices.how_marked: Quotations from the letter are introduced by verse references such as Phil 1,7, Phil 2,7, Phil 2,16, Phil 3,8a, Phil 3,8b, Phil 3,13, Phil 4,2.

key_terms.sense: Humility, the virtue Paul seeks to instill in the Philippian clergy.
Pride or self-inflation, the vice that especially attacks those who live well.
The Philippians' steadfastness or firm stand in faith, which Paul uses as proof of the value of his sufferings.
In Philippians 2:7, Severianus argues it expresses intensity or fullness, not mere likeness.
Chaff or refuse; Paul counts his former gains as this compared to Christ, and Severianus uses it as an image for the temporary, preparatory elements of the law that are separated at Christ's coming.
Stalk or straw; in Severianus's image, the stalk represents the prophets that grew from the seed of Abraham's faith.
Ear of grain; in the image, the ear represents Christ, pre-announced in hidden form.
Seed; the seed of Abraham's faith from which the law, prophets, and Christ grew.
Root; in the image, the root represents the things in the law that grew from the seed of Abraham's faith.
The Mosaic law, which Severianus sees as a preparatory stage whose chaff-like elements were separated once Christ came.
Clergy, the intended audience of Philippians according to Severianus.
Laity, the group Severianus says Paul was not addressing.

scripture: Severianus cites Pauline epistles by traditional titles (Philippians, 1 Timothy) and refers to Old Testament figures and concepts without formal citations. Modern citations should use standard English Bible book names and verse numbering.
uncertain: The exact date of composition is unknown.
The precise source of the tradition identifying Euodia as the jailer's wife and Syntyche as the man is not identified.
The original extent of the commentary is unknown; only fragments survive.

_unresolved_facts.claim: He interprets Paul's counting his former gains as loss and rubbish through an extended agricultural image: Abraham's faith is like the seed producing the root of the law, the stalk of the prophets, and the grain that is Christ
_unresolved_facts.source_quote: ἀπὸ τῆς πίστεως τοῦ Ἀβραὰμ ὡσπερεὶ ἀπὸ σπόρου ἡ ἀπὸ τῶν ἐν νόμῳ, καὶ ἡ καλάμη τῶν προφητῶν καὶ ὁ στάχυς ἤδη τὸν Χριστὸν ἐν τῷ κρυπτῷ προκαταγγέλλων
_unresolved_facts.fix: Abraham's faith is like the seed; the root is 'those in the law' (ἡ ἀπὸ τῶν ἐν νόμῳ), not 'the law' itself as a root. The stalk is the prophets, and the grain is Christ.

_unresolved_facts.claim: while the chaff-like elements of the law were separated at Christ's first coming
_unresolved_facts.source_quote: ὁ δὲ τούτων θερισμὸς καὶ ὁ ἁλοητὸς ἐν τῇ πρώτῃ παρουσίᾳ τοῦ σωτῆρος, οὗ τὸ πτύον ἐν τῇ χειρὶ καὶ διακαθαριεῖ τὴν ἅλωνα
_unresolved_facts.fix: The harvest and threshing of the stalk/prophets and grain/Christ occur at Christ's first coming; the separation of chaff-like elements (circumcision, sabbath-keeping) is described in u01-rem-close, not at the first coming itself.

_unresolved_facts.claim: He develops an agricultural image in which Abraham's faith is like the seed producing the root of the law, the stalk of the prophets, and the grain that is Christ; the harvest and threshing occur at Christ's first coming.
_unresolved_facts.fix: He develops an agricultural image in which Abraham's faith is like the seed producing 'those in the law' as the root, the stalk of the prophets, and the grain that is Christ; the harvest and threshing occur at Christ's first coming.

_unresolved_facts.claim: He concludes the agricultural image by clarifying that the stalk of the law did not cease, but circumcision, sabbath-keeping and other things were separated like chaff
_unresolved_facts.source_quote: οὔτε λοιπὸν ἐπαύσατο μὲν ἡ καλάμη τοῦ νόμου, ὥσπερ δὲ σκύβαλον ἐχωρίσθη περιτομή, σαββάτων τήρησις καὶ τῶν ἄλλων
_unresolved_facts.fix: He concludes the agricultural image by clarifying that the stalk of the law did not cease, but circumcision, sabbath-keeping and other things were separated like rubbish/skubalon (not chaff—the term is σκύβαλον, dung/refuse, not chaff).

_unresolved_facts.claim: Syntyche ... some say he was the man, likely the jailer himself
_unresolved_facts.fix: Syntyche ... some say he was the man (τὸν ἄνδρα). The brief adds 'likely the jailer himself' as speculation not in the source; the source only says 'the man' without identifying him as the jailer.

_unresolved_facts.claim: Timothy ... mentioned as the recipient of similar advice
_unresolved_facts.source_quote: καὶ τῷ Τιμοθέῳ δὲ γράφει· ἔπεχε σεαυτῷ, ἀντὶ τοῦ πρόσεχε σεαυτῷ
_unresolved_facts.fix: Timothy ... mentioned as the recipient of a letter where 'ἔπεχε σεαυτῷ' is used equivalently to 'πρόσεχε σεαυτῷ', illustrating the intensifying use of ὡς.
